title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: What is System Design?
summary: System design is the process of defining the architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data flow of a system so that it satisfies specified functional and non-functional requirements under real-world constraints.
objectives: What is the difference between system design and system architecture?
Why do interviewers say there is "no right answer" in system design?
What is the "scale ladder" and why is it useful?
What is back-of-the-envelope estimation and what numbers should you always compute?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** System design is the process of defining the architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data flow of a system so that it satisfies specified functional and non-functional requirements under real-world constraints.

System design sits between vague product ideas and concrete code. When a product manager says "build me a URL shortener," an engineer cannot simply start typing `app.post('/shorten', ...)`. They first have to decide what components exist, where state lives, how the components talk to each other, how the system behaves when 10 or 10 million users show up, and what happens when disks fail at 3 a.m. System design is the disciplined act of answering those questions before writing production code. It forces you to make assumptions explicit, to quantify capacity, and to expose trade-offs that would otherwise stay hidden until a pager goes off. In an interview setting, system design is also a test of communication: can you decompose an ambiguous problem, justify choices, and accept feedback without rewriting the whole architecture on the whiteboard?

What makes system design hard — and interesting — is that there is almost never a single "right" answer. Every choice is a trade-off. A relational database gives you strong consistency but limits horizontal write scaling. A NoSQL store scales writes easily but pushes consistency burden into application code. Caching improves read latency but introduces staleness and cache-invalidation bugs. Synchronous RPCs are simple to reason about but create tight coupling and cascading failures. Asynchronous events decouple producers from consumers but make failure debugging harder. The job of a designer is to choose the smallest set of trade-offs that still meets the requirements, document them, and revisit them as requirements evolve. A design that is "correct" today can become wrong six months later when traffic grows 10x or when a new regulatory constraint appears.

Real systems evolve through this trade-off treadmill visibly. Twitter is a textbook example. The original 2006 architecture was a single Ruby on Rails monolith backed by MySQL, running on a handful of servers. That architecture was wonderfully productive for a small team shipping features, but it struggled badly as the user base grew into the tens of millions: the timeline fan-out query (`SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE user_id IN (...) ORDER BY created_at DESC`) became catastrophic. Twitter responded in stages — first sharding MySQL by user, then introducing a custom JVM-based timeline service, then moving the write path to a distributed Manhattan/Gizzard store, then introducing Blender for search and Rainbird for analytics. Each step traded simplicity for capacity or latency. None of those decisions were "right" or "wrong" in isolation; they were the cheapest reasonable move given the constraint of the moment and the cost of migration.

A useful mental model for system design is the **scale ladder**: 1 user, 1 thousand users, 1 million users, 1 billion users. At 1 user, a laptop running Flask is enough. At 1 thousand users, you add a load balancer and a managed database. At 1 million users, you add a cache tier, a CDN, read replicas, and split monoliths into services. At 1 billion users, you are running a globally distributed system with multi-region active-active failover, dedicated storage engines, and tiered caches. The discipline is recognizing which rung you are on and designing only one rung ahead — over-engineering for a billion users on day one is as costly as under-engineering.

A second mental model is **back-of-the-envelope estimation**. Before drawing any boxes, a designer should estimate queries per second (QPS), storage per day, bandwidth, and the size of the working set. These numbers drive every later decision: cache hit rate needed, number of database shards, CDN egress bill, and whether a single Kafka partition can keep up. Without these estimates, "should we shard?" becomes a religious debate; with them, it becomes arithmetic. Throughout the rest of Phase 1, we will keep returning to these numbers because they are the bridge between abstract requirements and concrete components.

Pitfalls are everywhere. The most common is **resume-driven design**: picking Kafka, Kubernetes, and Cassandra because they sound impressive, when a single Postgres instance would have lasted years. Another is **ignoring failure modes**: designers draw happy-path diagrams and never ask what happens when a node dies, when a network partitions, or when a downstream dependency takes 30 seconds instead of 30 milliseconds. A third is **conflating scale with complexity**: many systems that look "distributed" are actually a single primary with replicas, and pretending otherwise wastes engineering effort. Good system design stays humble about which problems are actually hard.

System design connects to every other concept in this curriculum. Functional and non-functional requirements (Topic 2) are the inputs. Scalability (Topic 3) and availability (Topic 4) are the two most common non-functional goals. Later phases — networking, databases, caching, load balancing, message queues, microservices, observability — are all tools you compose to realize the design. The skill you are building is not memorizing components; it is learning to pick the right ones, justify them, and reason about their interactions under load and failure.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Product Idea] --> B[Requirements Gathering]
    B --> C{Functional?}
    C -->|What it does| D[Features, APIs, Data Model]
    C -->|How it behaves| E[NFRs: Scale, Latency, Avail]
    D --> F[Back-of-Envelope Estimate]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Component Architecture]
    G --> H[Trade-off Analysis]
    H --> I[Detailed Design]
    I --> J[Implementation]
    J --> K[Operate & Iterate]
    K -.feedback.-> B
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
+-------------+        +-----------------+        +------------------+
| Product     |  --->  | Requirements    |  --->  | Capacity         |
| Idea        |        | FR + NFR        |        | Estimates (QPS)  |
+-------------+        +-----------------+        +------------------+
                                                          |
                                                          v
+-------------+        +-----------------+        +------------------+
| Code &      | <---  | Trade-off       |  <---  | Architecture     |
| Operate     |        | Selection       |        | Components+Data  |
+-------------+        +-----------------+        +------------------+
```

### Walkthrough
1. Start from a fuzzy product idea and extract both functional (what it does) and non-functional (how it behaves) requirements.
2. Translate those requirements into rough capacity numbers — QPS, storage, bandwidth — using back-of-the-envelope math.
3. Pick components (load balancers, databases, caches, queues) that fit the numbers, explicitly writing down the trade-off each pick accepts.
4. Iterate as the system operates and requirements shift; the design is never "done."

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Back-of-the-envelope estimation helper.
# Toy implementation — illustrates the kind of arithmetic system designers
# do on a whiteboard before drawing any architecture boxes.

UNITS = {"": 1, "K": 1e3, "M": 1e6, "B": 1e9, "T": 1e12}

def parse_num(s: str) -> float:
    s = s.strip().upper()
    for suffix, mult in sorted(UNITS.items(), key=lambda x: -len(x[0])):
        if suffix and s.endswith(suffix):
            return float(s[:-len(suffix)]) * mult
    return float(s)

def fmt(n: float) -> str:
    for suffix, mult in [("T", 1e12), ("B", 1e9), ("M", 1e6), ("K", 1e3)]:
        if n >= mult:
            return f"{n/mult:.2f}{suffix}"
    return f"{n:.0f}"

def estimate(dau: str, requests_per_user: int, payload_kb: int,
             read_write_ratio: str = "10:1"):
    users = parse_num(dau)
    rw = read_write_ratio.split(":")
    reads, writes = int(rw[0]), int(rw[1])
    total = int(rw[0]) + int(rw[1])

    daily_requests = users * requests_per_user
    qps_avg = daily_requests / 86400
    qps_peak = qps_avg * 3  # rule of thumb: peak ~= 3x average
    write_qps = qps_peak * writes / total
    read_qps = qps_peak * reads / total

    daily_storage_gb = (write_qps * 86400 * payload_kb) / (1024 * 1024)
    yearly_storage_tb = daily_storage_gb * 365 / 1024

    bandwidth_mbps = (qps_peak * payload_kb * 8) / 1000

    print(f"DAU                       : {fmt(users)}")
    print(f"Avg QPS (all)             : {fmt(qps_avg)}")
    print(f"Peak QPS (3x avg)         : {fmt(qps_peak)}")
    print(f"  - Read QPS              : {fmt(read_qps)}")
    print(f"  - Write QPS             : {fmt(write_qps)}")
    print(f"Storage / day             : {fmt(daily_storage_gb)} GB")
    print(f"Storage / year            : {fmt(yearly_storage_tb)} TB")
    print(f"Peak bandwidth           : {fmt(bandwidth_mbps)} Mbps")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example: a Twitter-like app, 50M DAU, 30 actions/user/day, 1KB payload
    estimate("50M", requests_per_user=30, payload_kb=1, read_write_ratio="10:1")
```

quiz.explanation: System architecture describes the static structure of a system — which components exist, what their responsibilities are, and how they are connected (for example: "API gateway → service mesh → microservices → managed Postgres with read replicas").

quiz.question: Why do interviewers say there is "no right answer" in system design?
options: Five ms p99 rules out a synchronous network hop to a central database on every request — a single cache miss would blow the budget.
I start by refusing to design all of Netflix — I scope down to one slice, typically playback, because that is the part with the hardest NFRs.
Resume-driven design is choosing technologies because they look impressive on a CV rather than because they fit the problem — for example, picking Kafka, Kubernetes, and…
Because every concrete design is a bundle of trade-offs, and which trade-off is acceptable depends on requirements the interviewer has not fully stated.
quiz.explanation: Because every concrete design is a bundle of trade-offs, and which trade-off is acceptable depends on requirements the interviewer has not fully stated. Saying "use Kafka" is neither right nor wrong until you know the write throughput, the latency budget, the operational capacity of the team, and the consistency needs.
